strengths: Technically sound methodology combining MLE with Riemannian optimization and geometry-aware regularization, properly handling noise in different geometric settings
Comprehensive experimental validation across three datasets with thorough ablation studies varying noise levels and curvature, showing consistent (if modest) improvements
Excellent reproducibility: detailed pseudocode, hyperparameter specifications, hardware documentation, and code availability indicators
Effective visualizations (Figures 2-3, 5) that clearly demonstrate the method's ability to preserve geometric structure
Honest and explicit discussion of limitations including scalability constraints and acknowledgment of modest empirical gains
Well-motivated problem addressing real applications requiring non-Euclidean representations (cell cycles, phylogenetic trees, DNA analysis)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: using MLE with Riemannian optimization is straightforward application of standard techniques; main contribution (geometry-aware regularization) is relatively incremental
Modest empirical improvements: performance gains over ΔVAE often range 3-10% and sometimes fall within error bars (Table 1: Euclidean ℝ³ shows 0.55±0.04 vs 0.57±0.03)
Narrow experimental scope: all datasets are synthetic or pre-processed; no evaluation on real high-dimensional manifold benchmarks or standard graph datasets; only VAE-variant baselines

Unaddressed scalability limitations: paper acknowledges per-sample parametrization is prohibitive for large datasets but provides no solutions or large-scale experiments; no systematic runtime comparisons
Lack of theoretical analysis: no formal justification for when/why geometry-aware regularization improves learning, no convergence guarantees, no failure mode analysis
Test-time RGD latents strategy appears to be an optimization workaround without clear scalability or practical implementation details

strengths: Rigorous mathematical formulations with detailed ELBO derivations and explicit noise models for different geometric spaces (spherical, hyperbolic, etc.)
Comprehensive experimental setup with multiple manifold types tested and detailed reproducibility information in appendices (pseudocode, hyperparameters, hardware specs)
Good visualizations effectively demonstrating learned representations respecting geometric structures
Honest comparisons to established baselines (S-VAE, ΔVAE) with consistent experimental protocols across datasets
weaknesses: Empirical improvements are marginal and often within error bars (e.g., Table 1: 0.55±0.04 vs 0.53±0.04). No statistical significance testing provided despite overlapping confidence intervals, undermining the main claims.

Core contribution is incremental: applies existing Riemannian optimization techniques (geoopt) with a different training paradigm. Theoretical justification for why discarding the encoder improves performance is absent or weak.

Method requires per-sample latent optimization at test time (RGD inference), creating significant computational overhead compared to encoder-based approaches. This critical practical limitation is barely discussed.

Experimental scope insufficient: only 3 datasets (mostly small-scale), with cell cycle results showing mixed gains. No evaluation on standard benchmarks or recent geometric deep learning baselines beyond S-VAE and ΔVAE.
Unfair experimental comparison: comparing non-encoder generative model against VAE-based methods confounds architectural differences with methodological improvements.

Weak theoretical motivation: Why is MLE with Riemannian latents superior to encoder-based approaches? The ELBO derivation follows standard VAE theory but the method deviates without principled justification.

Limited novelty articulation: the paper reads as an implementation choice rather than a fundamental new insight. The relationship between core methodology and geometric regularization (Section E) feels disconnected.

Scalability concerns unaddressed: no computational complexity analysis, missing training time comparisons, serious practical limitations relegated to footnotes despite inference-time optimization being prohibitive for large datasets.

strengths: Principled geometric regularization: The noise-injection scheme is well-motivated through curvature-dependent scaling, with formal Taylor expansion justification. This moves beyond naive Riemannian optimization to genuinely geometry-aware learning.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Three real-world datasets (cell cycle, mtDNA sequences, branching diffusion), five manifold types, detailed ablations on noise scale effects, and proper reporting of error bars across five random seeds.

Clear technical execution: Well-structured methodology (Section 3) with accessible mathematical exposition; consistent improvements across diverse manifolds (Tables 1-3); effective visualizations (Figures 2-5) demonstrating learned representations respect geometric structure.

Strong reproducibility: Complete training details (hyperparameters, architectures, optimization schedules), hardware specifications, dataset sources with MIT licensing, pseudocode in appendices, and code availability promised.

Practical framework flexibility: Integration with geoopt enables application to arbitrary Riemannian manifolds; method requires only a decoder network with geometric regularization—simple to implement and extend.
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements: Test-set gains are small (cell cycle Pearson: often <0.05 over baselines; mtDNA F1: 0.35 absolute). For sphere S², test Pearson remains at 0.60 despite theoretical motivation. Unclear when practitioners should prefer this over existing methods.

Limited baseline comparisons: Comparisons restricted to S-VAE and ΔVAE (2018-2019). Missing recent hyperbolic/product space baselines from 2021-2025. Some baseline hyperparameters (P-VAE) required deferred implementation details.

Scalability validation absent: Only low-dimensional manifolds demonstrated (≤3D effective rank). Acknowledged computational challenges for high-dimensional manifolds not experimentally addressed. Real-world applicability for complex geometric data limited.

Incremental novelty: Core contribution—scaling noise by curvature factor Σ⁻¹—is a straightforward extension of Riemannian optimization combined with established regularization. Builds directly on Schuster & Krogh (2023) without substantial conceptual advance.

Test-time optimization cost not characterized: Method requires iterative MLE optimization per test sample (no pretrained encoder). Computational cost relative to inference in baselines not quantified, affecting practical deployment decisions.

strengths: Well-motivated encoder-less framework that elegantly sidesteps intractable manifold density estimation via Riemannian optimization and geometry-aware regularization
Solid mathematical derivation of the noise-based regularizer (Eqs. 11-16) showing how it implicitly incorporates Riemannian structure weighted by the metric tensor
Comprehensive experimental validation across three biologically distinct datasets (cyclic, hierarchical, evolutionary branching) with multiple manifold geometries
Excellent reproducibility with provided code/data, detailed experimental protocols, explicit hardware specifications, and hyperparameter documentation
Insightful ablation study (Figure 3c) demonstrating the accuracy-geometry tradeoff and providing practical guidance for regularization strength tuning
Generally competitive results showing consistent improvements over S-VAE and ∆VAE baselines in correlation and reconstruction metrics
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty—primarily combines existing components (DGD framework, Riemannian optimization, smoothness regularization) without substantial innovation in individual parts

Modest empirical improvements lacking statistical rigor—no p-values, significance tests, or confidence intervals despite having multiple random initializations; many improvements are ≤0.10 in magnitude
Outdated baseline comparisons—only includes S-VAE (2018) and ∆VAE (2019), missing recent hyperbolic and geometry-aware representation learning methods from 2020-2025
Critical hyperparameter tuning opacity—appendix states parameters were 'tuned for each model and dataset' without specifying validation procedures, risking bias toward the proposed method
Theoretical gaps in regularizer derivation—Taylor expansion ignores O(‖ε‖⁴) terms without discussing failure regimes; trace approximation of Hessian (Eq. 16) may lose important geometric structure

Questionable evidence of meaningful geometry learning—Table 1 shows nearly identical performance across fundamentally different manifolds (Euclidean, Sphere, Torus) for cell cycle data, raising whether geometric constraints are actually learned or method is robust to incorrect manifold choice

Weak generative quality and downstream utility—RGD discrimination scores (0.38-0.63) suggest poor distribution learning; downstream classification accuracy modest (0.31-0.90) using only simple linear models
Scalability limitations—experiments limited to ≤50D; Table 4 shows methods 'break' computationally; no analysis of memory scaling or applicability to high-dimensional problems

Incomplete experimental methodology—no initialization/seed sensitivity analysis, unfair UMAP comparison (dimensionality reduction vs. generative model), visualization quality issues, and limited exploration of failure modes

Unclear method applicability and presentation—weak justification that encoder-less approach avoids density estimation (regularizer acts as latent density prior); three case studies don't provide unified insights about when practitioners should use this method

strengths: Well-executed experimental methodology with multiple random seeds, proper train/val/test splits, and detailed reproducibility information in appendices
Mathematically sound derivation of geometric regularization approach (Equations 11-16) showing how manifold-valued noise induces the proposed regularization
Comprehensive treatment of three distinct biological datasets (cell cycle, branching diffusion, mitochondrial DNA) with clear data preprocessing details
Strong commitment to reproducibility with promised code/data release and detailed hyperparameters, hardware specifications, and training procedures
weaknesses: Central claims fundamentally contradicted by experimental results: Abstract claims 'much more scalable in high dimensions' but Table 4 shows the method breaks while baseline methods work; abstract claims improved reconstruction but Table 2 shows Euclidean R² outperforms the proposed hyperbolic/spherical variants

Marginal or no empirical improvements over baselines: Table 1 shows differences often within error margins; Table 2 demonstrates Euclidean outperforms proposed method (0.94 vs 0.86-0.91 Spearman); no statistical significance testing provided

Critical unexplained failure mode: Table 4 shows methods 'break' at higher latent dimensions while alternatives (ΔVar) scale successfully, but this methodological limitation is dismissed as computational rather than analyzed; directly undermines scalability claims

Limited novelty: Primarily combines existing DGD framework (Schüsser & Krogh 2023) with existing RiemannianAdam optimizer and straightforward Taylor-expansion-based noise analysis; no novel algorithmic insights
Fundamental question unaddressed: Results consistently suggest Euclidean embeddings work as well or better, but paper does not explain when/why the proposed geometric approach should be preferred

Weak downstream utility: Table 3 shows poor classification accuracy across all methods (many in 0.31-0.43 range), raising questions about whether learned representations are actually useful despite matching geometric properties
Inconsistent result interpretation: Figure 3a shows UMAP reveals clear tree structure despite text claiming it 'fails'; apparent contradictions between visualizations and narrative not resolved

Incomplete analysis of experimental design choices: Different reference sequences and preprocessing for different datasets (Appendices D-E) make cross-dataset comparisons difficult; no justification for why marginal improvements should justify added complexity

strengths: Novel methodology: Encoder-less generative model that directly optimizes Riemannian manifold-valued latents is a creative departure from standard VAE architectures
Original geometric regularization strategy using decoder Hessian information to adapt manifold geometry during training is genuinely novel and mathematically sound
Rigorous differential geometry foundation with proper use of Riemannian optimization, geodesic descent, and exponential maps for multiple manifold types (Euclidean, spheres, hyperbolic, tori)
Comprehensive experimental validation on three distinct biological datasets (cell cycle, branching diffusion, human mtDNA) with real practical applications
Honest and transparent limitations discussion: acknowledges modest improvements, trade-offs between local/global geometry, and cases where method matches baselines
Well-organized presentation with excellent visualizations effectively communicating learned representations
Extensive reproducibility support including detailed protocols, hyperparameters, hardware specs, and promised code/data availability
weaknesses: Empirical improvements often modest: Table 1 shows Pearson correlation differences of 0.01-0.05 across methods without statistical significance testing, making it unclear if improvements are meaningful
Theoretical justification for key approximations is incomplete: The claim that residuals are 'negligible on average' for unbiased estimates in Equation 15 lacks formal proof

Scalability claims are somewhat overstated: While computationally efficient, Table 4 timing results don't demonstrate dramatically better scaling than baselines; experiments limited to ~50D latent spaces
Missing principled guidance for hyperparameter selection: The noise scale σ strongly affects local-vs-global accuracy trade-off (Figure 3c) but paper provides limited guidance for practitioners
Theoretical analysis incomplete: No convergence guarantees, sample complexity bounds, or principled manifold selection criteria provided
Downstream utility evaluated only on simple tasks: Logistic regression and gradient boosting may not fully capture representation quality; more complex downstream tasks would strengthen claims

Limited ablation studies: No comparison of Riemannian Adam vs. alternatives, limited exploration of different manifold choices for same datasets, or comparison to simple baselines (PCA, direct clustering)
